tryit.text: How many times in a day, on a 12-hour clock, do the minute and hour hands form a straight line (an angle of 180°)?
tryit.think: Picture a real clock at 6:00. The hands make a straight line. When does it happen next?

tryit.text: Amat and Ankit each pick 3 different numbers from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Amat's sum is the highest possible, Ankit's the second highest. Which two numbers did both pick?
tryit.think: Start with Amat: which three numbers give the highest sum?

tryit.text: Sachin rolls a die until 6 appears three times. Each roll scores the number shown, and his total is 29. What is the minimum number of rolls he could have made?
tryit.think: Split it: three 6s give 18 points. How much is left, and how few rolls can make it?

tryit.text: The sum of three consecutive natural numbers is Y. Which number will Y always be divisible by?
tryit.think: Say it simply: “Add any three numbers in a row. What always divides the total?”

tryit.text: X is the sum of two or more DIFFERENT single-digit prime numbers. Which option CANNOT be a value of X?
tryit.think: I know the single-digit primes: 2, 3, 5 and 7. Which totals can they make?

tryit.text: X is the product of 2 single-digit prime numbers. Which statement is ALWAYS TRUE about X?
tryit.think: Ask why a statement could fail. Test it on the smallest and the biggest products, 2 × 2 and 7 × 7.

tryit.text: A two-digit number is 1 more than a multiple of 3. How many different possible values can it have?
tryit.think: Write the list: 10, 13, 16, … up to the largest two-digit one. Now count the steps of 3.

backcover_intro: In Class 6, children take Computational Thinking further: finding the rule behind number and shape patterns, testing ideas step by step and explaining why a method works. These are not just computer skills. They are thinking skills for every subject.
